fields.title: The Second Letter to the Corinthians
fields.subtitle: Pros Korinthious B, “Second to the Corinthians”
fields.description: The most personal of Paul’s letters, written after a painful visit and a letter written with many tears, to a church he loved and that had hurt him. Here is the God from whom all comfort comes; a ministry not of the written letter but of the Spirit, with faces uncovered, changed from glory to ever greater glory; treasure in pots made of clay; the message of reconciliation and a new creation in Christ; the grace of the Lord who, rich as he was, became poor; and, against rivals who boasted of their strength, an apostle who boasted of his weakness, a thorn in the flesh, and the answer “My grace is enough for you.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is 2 Corinthians?
qa.answer: The eighth book of the New Testament, a letter from the apostle Paul to the church in Corinth, written after 1 Corinthians. It celebrates a reconciliation between Paul and the church after a painful break, prepares them for a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and defends Paul’s ministry against rival teachers. Its great theme is that God’s power is seen in human weakness: “it is when I am weak that I am strong” (12:10).

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Corinthians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, together with Timothy, who is named in the first verse. Scholars of every school agree that Paul wrote it. He sent it from Macedonia, in northern Greece, probably around AD 55–56, after Titus had brought him the news that the Corinthians had repented and longed to see him again (7:5–7).

qa.question: What happened between 1 and 2 Corinthians?
qa.answer: The letter itself suggests the outline, though details are uncertain. Paul made a painful visit to Corinth (2:1), where someone wronged him; he then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), now usually called the tearful letter, and sent it with Titus. Anxious for news, he left Troas for Macedonia, where Titus met him with good news (2:12–13, 7:5–16). Meanwhile, rival teachers had arrived in Corinth, whom Paul answers in chapters 10–13.

qa.question: Is 2 Corinthians one letter or several?
qa.answer: Christians and scholars differ. The tone changes sharply at chapter 10, chapters 8 and 9 both deal with the collection, and 6:14–7:1 seems to interrupt its context, so many scholars think the book joins two or more of Paul’s letters to Corinth, perhaps with chapters 10–13 as part of the tearful letter or a later one. Others argue that it is a single letter written over some time. No manuscript has it in any other form, and the church has always received it as one book.

qa.question: What was Paul’s thorn in the flesh?
qa.answer: No one knows. Paul says only that “a thorn in the flesh was given” to him, “a messenger of Satan”, to keep him from becoming too proud after a vision of paradise, and that he begged the Lord three times to remove it (12:7–8). Suggestions have included an illness or disability, perhaps of the eyes, persecution, a group of opponents and temptation. What Paul passes on is the Lord’s answer: “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness.”

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For the God who said, “Out of darkness light will shine,” is the one who shone in our hearts, to bring the light of the knowledge of God’s glory, the glory seen in the face of Christ. But we hold this treasure in pots made of clay, so that the power, great beyond measure, may be God’s and may not come from us.

— 2 Corinthians 4:6–7

Of all Paul’s letters, this is the one in which we come closest to the man himself. In 1 Corinthians he is a teacher answering questions. In 2 Corinthians he is a wounded friend, by turns grieving, relieved, tender, sarcastic and fierce. He tells of a hardship in Asia so heavy that he gave up hope of staying alive, of a letter written “with many tears”, of sleepless nights and shipwrecks, of being lowered from a city wall in a basket, of a vision of paradise he would rather not talk about, and of a “thorn in the flesh” that God would not take away.

And through all of it runs one discovery, which may be the deepest thing Paul ever wrote: that God’s power is not seen in spite of human weakness, but in it. The treasure is in pots made of clay, so that everyone can see the power is God’s.

What happened after 1 Corinthians

The letter itself lets us piece together much of what happened between Paul’s first surviving letter to Corinth and this one, though not every detail is certain.

Things did not go well. Paul made a short visit to Corinth that he calls a visit “bringing grief” (2:1), apparently because someone in the church opposed or insulted him and the church did not stand with him. He went away and, instead of returning as he had planned, wrote them a severe letter, out of “great affliction and anguish of heart” (2:4). Like the earlier letter of 1 Corinthians 5:9, this “tearful letter” has not survived, unless, as some think, part of it is preserved in 2 Corinthians 10–13. He sent it with Titus.

Then he waited. At Troas, where a door stood open for preaching, he could not settle because Titus had not come back, and he went on to Macedonia to look for him. There, at last, Titus arrived with good news: the church had grieved, repented, disciplined the man who had wronged Paul, and longed to see him again. Paul writes from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, with Timothy, in relief and gladness, to complete the reconciliation, to prepare them for the collection for Jerusalem, and to confront a new danger: visiting teachers who were winning the church away from him.

One letter or several?

Anyone who reads the letter straight through notices how much its tone changes. Chapters 1 to 9 are warm and full of comfort; chapters 10 to 13 are sharp, ironic and defensive. Chapters 8 and 9 both take up the collection, as if from the beginning. And 6:14–7:1 seems to interrupt an appeal that flows smoothly from 6:13 to 7:2.

Many scholars think that 2 Corinthians gathers more than one letter, or parts of letters, into a single book: perhaps chapters 10 to 13 are the tearful letter, or a later letter sent when fresh trouble broke out. Others hold that it is one letter, dictated over some time, perhaps with new news arriving before the last part was written, and that a pastor can move from relief over the many to alarm about the few. There are no manuscripts of the letter in any other form. Whatever its history, the church has always read it as one book, and its parts speak to one another: the weakness Paul describes in chapter 4 is the weakness he boasts of in chapter 12.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–7: reconciliation and the ministry of the new covenant. The God of all comfort; Paul’s changed plans and the tearful letter; a ministry of the Spirit, carried in clay pots; the hope of the resurrection body; the message of reconciliation; and joy at Titus’s news.
  • Chapters 8–9: the collection. The generosity of the poor churches of Macedonia, the grace of Christ who became poor, and the God who loves a giver who gives gladly.
  • Chapters 10–13: Paul and the “super-apostles”. A defence of his ministry against rivals, in which he is forced to boast, and boasts of his weaknesses.

The God of all comfort

Paul usually opens a letter by thanking God for its readers. Here he blesses God for comfort:

Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes. He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us.

— 2 Corinthians 1:3–4

The word for comfort, with its verb, comes ten times in five verses. It is not the comfort of an easy life. Paul has just been through a crisis in the province of Asia, perhaps in Ephesus, so severe that “we had given up hope even of staying alive.” He sees God’s purpose in it: “so that our confidence would rest, not on ourselves, but on God, who raises the dead.” The comfort he has received is meant to flow on to others, and that is the pattern of the whole letter: suffering and comfort, death and life, passed from Christ to the apostle and from the apostle to the church.

Some in Corinth had accused Paul of being unreliable, because he had changed his travel plans. His answer is to point to God’s faithfulness: “However many promises God has made, in him each one is ‘Yes.’” He stayed away, he explains, to spare them another painful visit. And now he urges them to forgive the man who caused the trouble, “or he may be swallowed up by grief that is more than he can bear.”

A ministry of the Spirit

The rivals in Corinth came with letters of recommendation. Paul needs none: “Our letter is you yourselves.” The Corinthians are a letter written “not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, and not on stone tablets but on tablets of flesh, on human hearts.” That phrase recalls the promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, of a new covenant written on the heart, and Paul draws the contrast out: “For the written letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Chapter 3 then turns to Moses, who came down from Sinai with his face shining and covered it with a veil. Paul reads the story as a picture of the old covenant’s glory, real but passing, and of the far greater glory of the new. “But the veil is lifted away whenever a person turns to the Lord.” The chapter ends with one of the great sentences of the New Testament:

But all of us, our faces uncovered, look upon the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and we are being changed into the same image we see, from glory to ever greater glory. That is how the Lord, who is the Spirit, works.

— 2 Corinthians 3:18

Treasure in clay pots

If that is the glory of the ministry, the minister himself hardly looks the part. Paul does not hide it. The treasure is held in common earthenware, the cheap pots of any household, so that no one will mistake whose power it is:

In every way we are under pressure, but not cornered; we are at a loss, but not utterly at a loss; we are hunted, but not deserted; we are thrown down, but not destroyed. Everywhere we go we carry the dying of Jesus in our bodies, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our bodies.

— 2 Corinthians 4:8–10

So Paul does not give up. “Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day.” He calls his sufferings, which he will list in chapter 11, troubles that “are light and last only a moment”, outweighed by an eternal glory. And he looks beyond death. The body is a tent, to be taken down; God has prepared “a house that no human hands have made, eternal, in heaven.” Meanwhile he groans, longing to be clothed with it, and holds the Spirit “as a down payment”, the first instalment of what is to come.

Readers differ on what Paul expects between death and resurrection in chapter 5, whether to “make our home with the Lord” at death, as many take 5:8 to mean, or to wait for the resurrection body, or both in turn. All agree that his hope is not to be free of a body, but to put on a new one, “so that life may swallow up all that is mortal.”

The message of reconciliation

Why does Paul go on, through all this? “It is the love of Christ that drives us on.” One died for all, so that those who live would live for him. And the result is a whole new order of things:

So if anyone is in Christ, that person is part of a new creation. The old things have gone, and look, new things have come into being.

— 2 Corinthians 5:17

Paul calls his work “the ministry of reconciliation”. God, in Christ, was reconciling the world to himself, not holding people’s trespasses against them, and he has made Paul and his companions his ambassadors: “we plead with you: be reconciled to God.” The reason they can say so is given in one compressed sentence that has been pondered by every generation of the church:

Christ had never known sin, yet for our sake God made him to be sin, so that, united with him, we might become God’s righteousness.

— 2 Corinthians 5:21

Christians have explained this exchange in different ways, whether “made him to be sin” means that Christ bore sin’s judgment, or that he became a sin offering, as some translate it. But its heart is plain: the sinless one was identified with sinners, so that sinners might be united with him and share God’s righteousness. And the time to receive it is not some later day: “Look: the day of salvation is here now.”

Then Paul turns the word of reconciliation on the Corinthians themselves. “Our heart has opened wide to take you in,” he says; “let your hearts open wide to us as well.” Chapter 7 tells, with obvious joy, how Titus came, and how their grief “in God’s way” had led to repentance. “Grief that follows God’s way produces repentance that leads to salvation, a repentance no one will ever regret.”

The grace of giving

Chapters 8 and 9 are the longest passage on money in the New Testament, and they are about grace from start to finish. Paul is gathering a gift from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and he wants Corinth to finish what it began a year before. The churches of Macedonia, in deep poverty, had begged to give. The model for all such giving is Christ:

After all, you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: rich as he was, he became poor for your sake, so that his poverty might make you rich.

— 2 Corinthians 8:9

The gift should be freely given, according to what one has, not what one lacks; it aims at a kind of equality, as when Israel gathered manna in the wilderness. “God loves a giver who gives gladly.” And Paul shows his care for honesty: the money will be carried by trusted delegates chosen by the churches, so that no one can accuse him of mishandling it. He ends not with a target but with praise: “Thanks be to God for his gift, which no words can describe!”

Boasting of weakness

With chapter 10 the tone changes. Some in Corinth say of Paul, “His letters are weighty and strong, but when he is here in person he is weak, and the way he speaks is contemptible.” Teachers have arrived who are polished speakers, proud of their Jewish credentials, ready to accept the church’s money and to lord it over them. Paul calls them, with heavy irony, the “super-apostles”, and in 11:13 he calls such people false apostles. Who exactly they were, and what they taught, scholars still debate.

Paul hates to compare himself with them, but the church has forced him to it, so he plays the fool and boasts. Only his boasting is upside down. Are they Hebrews? “So am I.” Are they servants of Christ? “I am a better one”, and the proof is a list not of successes but of sufferings: five floggings of the forty lashes less one, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night and a day adrift, dangers everywhere, hunger, cold, “my anxious care for all the churches.” He crowns the list with an escape from Damascus “in a rope basket”, which some readers see as a deliberate reversal of the Roman honour given to the first soldier over an enemy wall.

Then he tells, in the third person, of “a man in Christ” caught up fourteen years before to the third heaven, to paradise, who heard things beyond speaking. He will not boast of that. Instead he tells of what was given to keep him humble: “a thorn in the flesh”. What it was, no one knows. Suggestions have ranged from an illness or disability, perhaps of the eyes, to persecution, to opponents, to temptation. Paul asked three times for it to be taken away, and received an answer instead:

But he answered me, “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness.” So I will be all the happier to boast of my weaknesses, for then the power of Christ may spread its tent over me.

— 2 Corinthians 12:9

“For it is when I am weak that I am strong.” That is the key to the whole letter. The power of Christ, crucified in weakness and living by the power of God, rests on those who are weak with him.

The letter ends with a warning that Paul is coming a third time, a call for the Corinthians to test themselves, and a prayer that they will be mended and made whole. Its last verse is the blessing that churches across the world still use to close their worship, naming Father, Son and Spirit together.

How to read 2 Corinthians

Read it as a letter between people who love each other and have hurt each other. Paul’s emotions run high, and his sentences sometimes run on, break off or double back, as people’s do when they are moved. Do not try to tidy them too quickly.

Watch for the paired words that keep returning: affliction and comfort, death and life, weakness and power, poverty and riches, sorrow and joy. In almost every chapter Paul holds the two together, never pretending that the first has disappeared, always insisting that the second is stronger. And notice the questions behind the letter that are still ours: what makes a leader worth following, what real spiritual power looks like, and how a broken relationship in the church can be mended.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Corinthians are worth knowing about before you begin.

“A down payment.” Where older Bibles call the Spirit a “guarantee” or “earnest” (1:22, 5:5), this translation uses a plain commercial phrase, “a down payment”: the first instalment of what God will give in full, and the promise that the rest will come.

“Done away with.” In chapter 3 many Bibles say that the glory on Moses’ face was “fading”. This translation says it was “being done away with”, a glory brought to an end and not meant to last, which is how it reads the Greek verb Paul uses there and elsewhere.

“Pots made of clay” and “spread its tent”. In 4:7 the treasure is in “pots made of clay”, the everyday earthenware of the original. In 12:9, where older Bibles say the power of Christ may “rest upon” Paul, this translation keeps the picture in Paul’s verb, which is related to the word for a tent: the power of Christ may “spread its tent over me”, as God’s glory once dwelt in the tent in the wilderness.

“God’s holy people.” Those older Bibles call “saints” are here “God’s holy people”, so it is plain that Paul means every believer, as in the collection “for God’s holy people” in Jerusalem.

The last verses. Bibles number the end of the letter differently. In most English Bibles the greetings are 13:12–13 and the closing blessing is 13:14; in the Greek text, and some modern Bibles, the blessing is 13:13. This edition cites the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and from Timothy our brother, to the church of God in Corinth, together with all God’s holy people throughout Achaia. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

The God of all comfort

Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes. He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us. For as the sufferings of Christ overflow into our lives, so our comfort also overflows through Christ. If we are afflicted, it is so that you may be comforted and saved. If we are comforted, it is so that you may be comforted too, and that comfort works in you as you patiently endure the same sufferings we also suffer. So we have a firm hope for you. We know that you are partners in the sufferings, and so you are partners in the comfort too.

Rescued from death in Asia

We do not want you to be left unaware, brothers and sisters, of the hardship that came on us in Asia. We were weighed down so heavily, so far past our strength, that we had given up hope even of staying alive. In fact, we had accepted within ourselves that we were condemned to die. That was so that our confidence would rest, not on ourselves, but on God, who raises the dead. God rescued us from so great a death, and he will rescue us. We have fixed our hope on him that he will rescue us yet again, as you also work with us by praying for us. Then the gift God has given us through the prayers of many will be met with thanks from many people for our sake.

Here is what we take pride in, and our conscience confirms it: in the world at large, and still more with you, we have behaved with a holiness and sincerity that come from God, guided not by merely human wisdom but by the grace of God. We write you nothing other than what you can read and recognize as true. And I hope you will come to recognize it completely, as you have already recognized us in part: that we are your reason to be proud, as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.

Paul’s change of plans

Confident of this, I had planned to come to you first, to give you a second gift of grace. I would pass through your city on the way to Macedonia, return to you from Macedonia, and then let you help me on my journey to Judea. So when I planned this, did I treat it lightly? Or are my plans made by merely human standards, so that with me it is “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at once? But God is faithful, and our word to you is not “Yes” and “No” at once. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, whom Silvanus, Timothy and I proclaimed among you, did not turn out to be “Yes” and “No.” In him “Yes” has become a reality. However many promises God has made, in him each one is “Yes.” So it is through him too that we answer God with “Amen,” and God is given glory through us. It is God who makes us secure in Christ, us together with you. God anointed us, and God sealed us as his own and gave us the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.

I call on God as witness against my own life if I am not telling the truth: I held back from coming to Corinth again because I wanted to spare you. We do not mean that we are masters of your faith. Rather, we work alongside you to bring you joy, because you are standing firm in your faith.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 2
fields.body_html:
For I settled this in my own mind: I would not come to you again bringing grief. For if I grieve you, who is left to make me glad, except the very ones I have grieved? That is the very reason I wrote to you before: so that when I came I would not be grieved by the very people who ought to give me joy. For I was sure of every one of you, sure that what gives me joy gives joy to all of you. I wrote to you out of great affliction and anguish of heart, and with many tears. I did not write to make you grieve. I wrote so that you would come to know my love, which overflows toward you above all.

Forgiving the offender

Now if someone has caused grief, he has caused it not to me but to all of you, at least in part (I do not want to press the point too hard). The penalty that most of you imposed on this man is enough for him. So now you should turn the other way: forgive him and comfort him, or he may be swallowed up by grief that is more than he can bear. So I urge you to confirm your love for him openly. For this was another purpose of my writing: to learn whether you would prove yourselves true, obedient in every matter. If you forgive anyone anything, I forgive that person too. For whatever I have forgiven, so far as I have had anything to forgive, I have forgiven for your sake, in the presence of Christ, so that Satan does not gain the advantage over us. We know well enough what he has in mind.

No rest in Troas

When I came to Troas for the gospel of Christ, I found a door standing open for me in the Lord’s work. Even so, my spirit could not settle, because Titus my brother was nowhere to be found. So I took leave of the believers there and set out for Macedonia.

The fragrance of Christ

But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us along in his triumphal procession, and who through us makes known in every place the fragrance that is the knowledge of him. For to God we are the pleasing aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To some it is a fragrance of death that leads to death; to others, a fragrance of life that leads to life. And who is fit for a calling like this? For we are not like the many who trade in the word of God for gain. We speak with pure motives, as people from God, in the sight of God, in Christ.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 3
fields.body_html:
A letter from Christ

Are we starting to recommend ourselves all over again? Or do we need letters of introduction to you or from you, the way some people do? Surely not! Our letter is you yourselves. It is written in our hearts, and everyone can recognize it and read it. Plainly you are a letter from Christ, produced through our service. It was written not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, and not on stone tablets but on tablets of flesh, on human hearts.

This is the confidence we have before God, and it comes through Christ. Not that we are fit for this by our own resources, as if we could count anything as our own doing. Our fitness comes from God. He has made us fit to be servants of a new covenant, a covenant not of the written letter but of the Spirit. For the written letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The greater glory of the new covenant

The ministry of death, cut in letters into stone, still came with glory, so bright that the Israelites could not fix their eyes on Moses’ face because of the glory shining there, a glory that was being done away with. How much more, then, will the ministry of the Spirit come with glory! For if the ministry of condemnation had glory, the ministry of righteousness overflows with far more glory. Indeed, in this respect what was once glorified has no glory at all, outshone as it is by a glory far greater. For if what was being done away with had its glory, what remains has glory far greater still.

The veil taken away

So, since this is our hope, we speak with great openness, not as Moses did when he kept covering his face with a veil, so that the Israelites would not fix their eyes on the end of what was being done away with. Their minds, however, were made hard. Right up to the present day, the same veil stays in place when they hear the old covenant read, and it is not lifted, since it is in Christ that it is done away with. And still today, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. But the veil is lifted away whenever a person turns to the Lord. Now this Lord is the Spirit, and freedom is found wherever the Spirit of the Lord is. But all of us, our faces uncovered, look upon the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and we are being changed into the same image we see, from glory to ever greater glory. That is how the Lord, who is the Spirit, works.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 4
fields.body_html:
The light of the gospel

So, since we hold this ministry because God showed us mercy, we do not give up. We have refused the hidden ways that people are ashamed of. We do not act with trickery, and we do not dilute the word of God. Instead, we make the truth plain, and that is how we recommend ourselves to the conscience of every person, before God. If our gospel is veiled at all, it is veiled from those who are perishing. Among them the god of this age has blinded the minds of those who do not believe, so that they cannot see the light that shines out from the gospel, the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. For we do not preach about ourselves. We preach Christ Jesus as Lord, and we speak of ourselves only as your servants, for Jesus’s sake. For the God who said, “Out of darkness light will shine,” is the one who shone in our hearts, to bring the light of the knowledge of God’s glory, the glory seen in the face of Christ.

Treasure in clay pots

But we hold this treasure in pots made of clay, so that the power, great beyond measure, may be God’s and may not come from us. In every way we are under pressure, but not cornered; we are at a loss, but not utterly at a loss; we are hunted, but not deserted; we are thrown down, but not destroyed. Everywhere we go we carry the dying of Jesus in our bodies, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our bodies. For while we live, we are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’s sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our mortal flesh. So death is doing its work in us, but life is doing its work in you.

It is written, “I believed; that is why I spoke.” We have the same Spirit of faith as the one who wrote those words: we too believe, and that is why we too speak. For we know that the one who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus, and will bring us, together with you, into his presence. Everything is for your sake, so that grace, as it spreads through more and more people, may make thanks to God overflow and bring glory to God.

What cannot be seen

So we do not give up. Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day. Our troubles are light and last only a moment, and they are bringing about for us an eternal glory, weighty beyond all measure. All the while, we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen. What can be seen lasts only a while; what cannot be seen is eternal.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 5
fields.body_html:
Our eternal home in heaven

For we know that if the tent we live in here on earth is taken down, we have a building from God, a house that no human hands have made, eternal, in heaven. So in this tent we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven over the one we have, sure that once we have put it on we will not be found naked. While we are in this tent we groan under its weight. It is not that we want to take it off; we want to put the new one on over it, so that life may swallow up all that is mortal. It is God who has prepared us for this very thing, and he has given us the Spirit as a down payment.

So we always have courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we make our way by faith, not by sight. We have courage, then, and we would much rather move out of the body and make our home with the Lord. That is why we set our hearts on pleasing him, whether we are still at home in the body or have left it. For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what matches the things done in the body, whether good or worthless.

Driven by the love of Christ

Because we know the fear of the Lord, we set out to persuade people. God already sees us clearly for what we are, and I hope your consciences see us just as clearly. We are not recommending ourselves to you again. Rather, we are giving you a reason to be proud of us, so that you will have something to say to those who take pride in outward show and not in what is in the heart. If we are out of our mind, that is for God. If we are sensible, that is for you. It is the love of Christ that drives us on. We have reached this judgment: one has died on behalf of all, and so all have died. He died on behalf of all, so that those who live would no longer live for their own sake, but for the sake of the one who died and was raised on their behalf.

A new creation

So from now on we look at no one by merely human standards. Even if we once knew Christ by those standards, that is not how we know him now. So if anyone is in Christ, that person is part of a new creation. The old things have gone, and look, new things have come into being. And all of it is God’s doing. Through Christ he has reconciled us to himself, and he has given us the ministry of reconciliation. For it was God who, in Christ, was at work reconciling the world to himself. He did not hold their trespasses against them, and he has put the word of reconciliation in our keeping. So we are ambassadors who speak for Christ, and it is God himself who makes his appeal through us. Speaking for Christ, we plead with you: be reconciled to God. Christ had never known sin, yet for our sake God made him to be sin, so that, united with him, we might become God’s righteousness.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 6
fields.body_html:
Servants of God in hardship

So, as people who work together with God, we also appeal to you: do not let the grace of God you have received be wasted on you. For he says, “At a time of favor I answered you; on a day of salvation I came to your aid.” Look: the time of favor is here now. Look: the day of salvation is here now. We give no one any reason to stumble in anything, so that no fault can be found with our ministry. Instead, in everything we recommend ourselves as God’s servants do: with great endurance, in hardships, in calamities, in tight corners, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in toil, in sleepless nights, in going without food; by purity, by knowledge, by patience, by kindness, by the Holy Spirit, by love that is real, by speaking the truth, by the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left; in honor and in disgrace, in slander and in praise. We are taken for deceivers, yet we are honest; for unknowns, yet we are well known; for dying, and yet here we are, alive; for people under discipline, yet we are not put to death; for grieving, yet we are always full of joy; for poor, yet we bring riches to many; for people with nothing, yet everything is ours.

Open your hearts

Corinthians, we have spoken to you without holding back, and our heart has opened wide to take you in. You have all the room you need in us; it is in your own affections that you are cramped. Give us the same in return. I am speaking as I would to my children: let your hearts open wide to us as well.

The temple of the living God

Do not be unevenly yoked with unbelievers. Can righteousness and lawlessness be partners? Can light and darkness share anything? How can Christ be in agreement with Beliar? What share can a believer have together with an unbeliever? Can God’s temple come to terms with idols? We, after all, are the temple of the living God. As God has said, “I will make my dwelling in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people.” So “come out from among them and keep yourselves apart,” says the Lord, “and do not touch what is unclean; then I will take you in.” “I will be your Father, and you will be my sons and daughters,” declares the Lord Almighty.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 7
fields.body_html:
Dear friends, since these promises are ours, let us wash ourselves clean of every stain on body and spirit, and carry our holiness through to its goal as we live in the fear of God.

Make room for us

Open your hearts to us. We have done no wrong to anyone, brought no one to ruin, and cheated no one. I am not saying this to condemn you. I have told you before: you are in our hearts, and we are bound to you in death and in life. I can speak to you very openly, and I have every reason to be proud of you. Comfort fills me, and joy floods over me in spite of all our hardship.

Titus brings comfort

Even when we came to Macedonia, there was no relief for us in our human weakness. We met hardship at every turn: strife all around us, fear in our hearts. But God, who comforts those who are brought low, comforted us by bringing Titus to us. And it was not only his arrival that comforted us, but also the comfort he himself had found among you. He told us how you long for me, how you mourn over what happened, how eager you are to stand up for me. So my joy was greater still. So even if my letter grieved you, I do not regret it. I did regret it for a while, for I see that the letter grieved you, if only for a short time. Now, though, I rejoice. It is not your grief that makes me glad, but the fact that it brought you to repentance. You grieved in God’s way, and so you have lost nothing because of us. Grief that follows God’s way produces repentance that leads to salvation, a repentance no one will ever regret. But grief that follows the world’s way produces death. Think what this grieving in God’s way has done for you! How earnest it has made you, how eager to clear yourselves, how indignant, how alarmed, how full of longing, how zealous, how ready to see the wrong punished! In everything you have shown that you are clear of blame in this affair. So although I wrote to you, my aim was not the man who did the wrong, nor the one who was wronged. I wrote so that your earnest care for us would become plain to you yourselves, there in the sight of God. That is why we have been comforted.

The joy of Titus

And on top of our own comfort, we rejoiced even more over the joy Titus had, because all of you had put his spirit at ease. I had spoken proudly of you to him, and you did not let me down. We have always spoken the truth to you, and in the same way the proud things we said about you to Titus have turned out to be the truth. His deep love goes out to you all the more when he recalls how every one of you obeyed, and how you welcomed him with fear and trembling. I rejoice that in every way I can rely on you.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 8
fields.body_html:
Generous giving in Macedonia

We want you to know, brothers and sisters, about the grace God has given to the churches of Macedonia. Hardship has put them to a severe test, yet their joy has overflowed, and their deep poverty has spilled over into riches of generosity. I can vouch for it: they gave all they could, and more than they could, and they did it of their own free will. Again and again they appealed to us, begging for the favor of a share in the relief for God’s holy people. It went beyond anything we had hoped for. Before anything else they gave themselves to the Lord, and then, because God willed it, to us. That is why we have asked Titus, who got this started among you in the first place, to see this gift of grace through to the end with you as well. You overflow in everything else: faith, speech, knowledge, eagerness of every kind, and the love from us that now lives in you. Now see that you overflow in this gift of grace as well.

The grace of giving

I am not giving you an order. I am using the eagerness of others to put your love to the test and show that it is real. After all, you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: rich as he was, he became poor for your sake, so that his poverty might make you rich. I offer my advice on this, because it is in your interest. You made a start last year, ahead of others, and it was not only a matter of doing something: you wanted to do it. Now bring the doing of it to an end as well. You were eager to want it; let the finishing show the same eagerness, giving out of whatever you have. When eagerness is there, a gift is welcomed for what the giver has, not judged by what the giver lacks. The point is not to bring relief to others by bringing hardship on you. It is a matter of equality. At this moment your surplus can meet their need, so that one day their surplus may meet yours. That way there is equality. As it is written, “The one who gathered a lot had nothing extra, and the one who gathered a little did not go short.”

Titus and the brothers

But thanks be to God, who fills the heart of Titus with the same eager concern for you that I feel. Titus welcomed our request, but more than that, he is so keen that he is setting out to you by his own choice. Traveling with Titus is the brother whose work for the gospel has won him praise in all the churches; we are sending him too. Not only that: the churches voted to appoint him as our companion on the journey, as we take charge of this gift of grace. We do it to bring glory to the Lord himself, and because we are eager to help. We are guarding against any charge that could be brought against us over this large sum we are handling. Our concern is for what is honorable, both before the Lord and before people. With them we are also sending our brother. Time after time and in many situations we have put him to the test and found him eager, and he is more eager than ever now, because he has great confidence in you. If anyone asks about Titus: he is a partner of mine, working with me for you. If they ask about our brothers: they are envoys of the churches, and they bring glory to Christ. So, with the churches looking on, give these men proof of your love, and let them see why we have been proud of you.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 9
fields.body_html:
Ready before Paul comes

There is really no need for me to write to you about the relief for God’s holy people. I know how willing you are, and I speak of it with pride to the Macedonians: “Achaia has been ready since last year.” Your zeal has spurred most of them into action. The reason I am sending the brothers is so that our pride in you does not prove hollow on this point, and so that you are ready, as I kept saying you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians travel with me and discover that you are not ready, we would be put to shame for having been so confident, to say nothing of you. That is why I felt I had to ask the brothers to travel to you ahead of me and to put in order beforehand the generous gift you promised, so that it will be ready as a gift of generosity, not as a gift of greed.

Sowing generously

Keep this in mind: sow sparingly and you will reap sparingly; sow generously and you will reap generously. Each of you should give the amount you have settled on in your own heart, not with regret and not because you feel you must. God loves a giver who gives gladly. God is able to make all grace abound for you, so that in every way and at all times you will have everything you need, with plenty to spare for every good work. As it is written: “He has scattered his gifts far and wide and given to people in need; his righteousness lasts forever.” God, who provides seed for the sower and bread to eat, will provide you with seed as well, and multiply it, and make your righteousness yield a bigger harvest. You will be made rich in every way so that you can be generous in every way, and your generosity, carried by us, will bring about thanksgiving to God. For this relief, a sacred service, not only fills up what God’s holy people lack; it also overflows in many thanksgivings to God. This relief will show what you are, and they will give glory to God for it: for the way you submit to the gospel of Christ that you confess, and for the generosity of your partnership with them and with everyone. And when they pray for you, they will long for you, because of the surpassing grace of God that rests on you. Thanks be to God for his gift, which no words can describe!

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 10
fields.body_html:
Paul defends his authority

I, Paul, make this appeal to you myself, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. I am the one who is humble when I am with you in person, but bold with you when I am at a distance. I beg you not to make me show boldness when I am with you, the confidence that I count on using against some people, those who count us as living by merely human standards. We do live as human beings, but we do not fight our battles by merely human standards. Our weapons in this fight are not merely human; they have power from God to tear down strongholds, and so we tear down arguments and every proud tower raised against the knowledge of God. We capture every thought and lead it away to obey Christ. We are prepared to punish all disobedience, once you yourselves have fully obeyed.

Look at what is right in front of you. Anyone who is confident of belonging to Christ should think again and consider this: just as that person belongs to Christ, so do we. Suppose I boast rather more than I should about our authority, which the Lord gave us to build you up and not to tear you down: I will not be put to shame. I would not want it to look as though I were out to terrify you by letter. For someone says, “His letters are weighty and strong, but when he is here in person he is weak, and the way he speaks is contemptible.” Anyone who says this should understand that we are the same in action when we are with you as we are in the words of our letters when we are away.

Boasting within the measure God gives

We would not dare to put ourselves in the same class as some of those who recommend themselves, or to set ourselves beside them. They use themselves as the measuring stick and compare themselves with themselves, and that shows how little they understand. But we will not boast of things outside our measure. We will boast only within the measure of the field that God has measured out to us as ours, and it reaches even as far as you. We are not overstretching ourselves, as we would be if our field did not reach you; we did reach you, bringing the gospel of Christ. We do not boast of things outside our measure, in work that others have done. We hope instead that as your faith grows, we will be given far more room among you, still within our field, so that we can carry the gospel to the lands beyond you, without boasting of ground someone else has already prepared.

But, as Scripture says, “Whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.” The person who stands approved is not the one who recommends themselves, but the one the Lord recommends.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 11
fields.body_html:
Paul and the false apostles

I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. Yes, do bear with me. My jealousy for you is the jealousy of God himself. I have pledged you in marriage to one husband: I mean to bring you to Christ as a pure virgin bride. Yet I fear that, in the way the serpent’s cunning tricked Eve, your minds may somehow be spoiled and turned away from simple, pure loyalty to Christ. When anyone turns up and preaches another Jesus than the one we preached, or you take in a spirit unlike the one you received, or a gospel unlike the one you welcomed, you tolerate it splendidly! I count myself not one bit behind the super-apostles. Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not so in knowledge. We have shown you that plainly, in every way and in all things.

Or was it a sin on my part to lower myself so that you could be lifted up, by proclaiming God’s gospel to you without charging you anything? I plundered other churches, accepting pay from them so that I could serve you. And while I was there with you and ran short, I was a weight on no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia made up what I lacked. In every way I have made sure I cost you nothing, and I will keep it that way. I declare by the truth of Christ that is in me: this boast of mine will not be silenced anywhere in the districts of Achaia. Why so? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!

And I will go on doing what I am doing, to deny an opening to those who look for one: an opening to boast that they are on the same footing as we are. People like that are false apostles and dishonest workers, passing themselves off as apostles of Christ. No surprise there: Satan himself passes himself off as an angel of light. So it is no great thing if his servants also pass themselves off as servants of righteousness. Their end will match what they have done.

Paul boasts like a fool

Once more I say it: nobody should think I am a fool. Otherwise, welcome me even as a fool, so that I can boast a little too. What I say with this confidence in boasting is not said in the Lord’s way, but as it were in foolishness. Since many are boasting by merely human standards, I will boast too. You are wise people, after all, and so you happily bear with fools! Indeed you put up with it if someone holds you in bondage, if someone eats you up, if someone takes you in, if someone lords it over you, if someone hits you in the face. I must say, to our shame, that we have been far too weak to act like that! But whatever anyone else dares to boast of (I am talking in foolishness), I dare to boast of it too. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I. Are they servants of Christ? I am talking as if I had lost my mind, but I am a better one: with far more labors, far more imprisonments, beatings past counting, and brushes with death again and again. Five times the Jewish authorities gave me the forty lashes less one. Three times I was flogged with rods; once I was stoned; three times my ship was wrecked; a night and a day I have spent out on the deep. Again and again I have been on the road, facing dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the open country, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers and sisters; in labor and weariness, many nights without sleep, in hunger and thirst, many days going without food, in cold and with too little to wear. And apart from all these other things, there is what presses on me day after day: my anxious care for all the churches. Is anyone weak without my feeling weak as well? Is anyone made to fall without my burning inside? If boast I must, my boasting will be about the things that belong to my weakness. The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, the one who is blessed for all ages, knows that what I say is no lie. In Damascus, the ruler appointed by King Aretas set a watch on the city of the Damascenes to catch me. But I was let down through an opening in the wall in a rope basket, and I escaped from his grasp.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 12
fields.body_html:
Visions and a thorn in the flesh

I have to boast. It does no good, but now I will turn to visions and revelations given by the Lord. Fourteen years ago a man I know, a man in Christ, was snatched away as far as the third heaven. Whether this happened in the body or outside the body, I do not know. God knows. This same man, I know (in the body or apart from it, I do not know; God knows), was snatched away into paradise. There he heard things beyond speaking, which no human being is allowed to tell. About a man like that I will boast, but about myself I will boast only of my weaknesses. Should I decide to boast, that would not make me a fool, since it would be the truth I spoke. But I hold back. I do not want anyone to think more of me than what they see in me or hear from me, or to think more of me because the revelations were so extraordinary. So, to stop me from becoming too proud, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan, sent to beat me down, to stop me from becoming too proud. I begged the Lord three times about this, asking that it would leave me. But he answered me, “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness.” So I will be all the happier to boast of my weaknesses, for then the power of Christ may spread its tent over me. That is why I am glad to have weaknesses, insults, calamities, persecutions and tight corners, for the sake of Christ. For it is when I am weak that I am strong.

Paul’s concern for the Corinthians

I have become a fool. You forced me into it. It was you who should have been recommending me. In nothing did I fall short of these super-apostles, even if I am nothing. Among you, with all endurance, the signs that mark an apostle were done: signs, wonders and deeds of power. In what way were you put at a disadvantage compared with the other churches, except that I myself never lived off you? Please forgive me for this injustice!

Ready to come a third time

Here I am, ready to come to you for the third time, and I will not live off you. I am not after your money; I am after you. It is not for children to put money aside for their parents; it is parents who put it aside for their children. For my part, I will gladly spend everything I have, and spend myself to the last, for your sake. If I love you so much more, does that mean you love me less? Granted, I myself did not weigh you down. Still, some say I was cunning and caught you with a trick. Take any one of those I have sent to you: did I use any of them to cheat you? I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not cheat you, did he? Did we not conduct ourselves in the same spirit? Did we not tread in the same footsteps? Have you supposed this whole time that we are pleading our case before you? We are speaking in the sight of God, as those who are in Christ. Everything we do, dear friends, is to build you up. For I fear that I may come and find you other than I wish, and that you may find me other than you wish. I fear there may be quarreling, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalry, slander, whispering behind backs, people puffed up with pride, and disorder. I fear that when I come, my God may again bring me low in front of you, and that I may have to mourn over many who sinned in the past and still have not repented of what they did: impurity, sexual immorality and indecency.

fields.title: 2 Corinthians 13
fields.body_html:
I am now coming to you for the third time. “Every charge is to be settled on what two or three witnesses say.” When I was with you on my second visit, I gave a warning to those who had sinned before and to all the rest, and now, while I am away, I give it again: when I come back I will spare no one, since you are asking for evidence that Christ really speaks in me. He does not deal with you in weakness; he is powerful among you. He was indeed crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God. We too are weak in him, but you will find us living with him by the power of God.

Test yourselves

Look closely at yourselves: are you holding to the faith? Put yourselves to the test. Or do you not see in your own lives that Jesus Christ is in you? That is, unless you fail the test. And I hope you will see that we are not the ones who fail the test. Our prayer to God is that you will do no wrong at all. Our aim is not to look as though we have passed the test; we want you to do what is good, even if we then look like people who have failed it. We have no power to act against the truth, only to act for it. We are glad to be weak if it means that you are strong. Indeed, we pray for this: that you will be mended and made whole. That is why I am writing this while I am still away: so that when I come I need not deal with you sharply, using the authority the Lord gave me, which is for building up and not for tearing down.

Final appeal, greetings and blessing

Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice. Let yourselves be mended, be encouraged, be of one mind, and keep the peace among you. Then the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All God’s holy people send you greetings. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with every one of you.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with every one of you.

— 2 Corinthians 13:14

A letter that began with grief, misunderstanding and tears ends with a blessing on “every one of you”. Paul has rebuked the Corinthians, pleaded with them, mocked their rivals and laid his own heart bare. But his last word is a prayer that they will know the grace of Christ, the love of the Father and the fellowship of the Spirit, the one God in whose life a broken church can be made whole. It is no accident that churches still close their worship with it. Every congregation, sooner or later, needs what Corinth needed.

The question the letter leaves

The Corinthians wanted a leader who looked strong: impressive in person, eloquent, confident, successful. 2 Corinthians asks what strength really is. Paul’s answer is a man lowered from a wall in a basket, a body carrying “the dying of Jesus”, a prayer three times refused. And yet through that man the light of the knowledge of God’s glory reached Corinth.

The question is not only about leaders. It reaches every believer who has prayed for a thorn to be taken away and found it still there. Paul does not say the thorn is good, or that the prayer was wrong. He says that the answer he received was better than the one he asked for: “My grace is enough for you.” The letter does not promise that weakness will be removed. It promises that it will not have the last word.

Where the letter points

It points, first, to the cross and the resurrection, not as doctrines only but as the shape of Christian life. Christ “was indeed crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God”, and those who belong to him share both: dying and yet alive, sorrowful and yet always full of joy, poor and yet making many rich.

It points, second, to reconciliation. The God who reconciled the world to himself in Christ gave his people a ministry of reconciliation, and Paul practised it on the church that had hurt him. He forgave, urged them to forgive the man who had wronged him, and opened his heart wide. The gospel he preached to the world, he lived in the church.

And it points to what cannot yet be seen. “What can be seen lasts only a while; what cannot be seen is eternal.” The tent will come down, and a house not made with hands is waiting. That is why Paul did not give up, and why his readers need not either.

Where to go from here

Many preachers have found in this letter words for the suffering and the weary, and a number of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On comfort in affliction (chapter 1). Hannah Whitall Smith’s The God of All Comfort, whose title chapter opens with 1:3–4, and Charles H. Spurgeon’s Consolation Proportionate to Spiritual Sufferings (1:5).
  • On being changed into his image (chapter 3). Henry Drummond’s The Changed Life (3:18), and in A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, the New Testament volume, the chapter “The Holy Spirit in Second Corinthians”.
  • On the things that are not seen (chapter 4). Alexander Maclaren’s Looking at the Unseen and Thomas Chalmers’s The Transitory Nature of Visible Things, both on 4:18.
  • On the love of Christ and the call to be reconciled (chapter 5). Maclaren’s The Love that Constrains (5:14) and Samuel Davies’s Sinners Entreated to Be Reconciled to God (5:20).
  • On godly sorrow (chapter 7). Frederick W. Robertson’s The Power of Sorrow (7:10).
  • On spiritual warfare and strength in weakness (chapters 10–12). Simpson’s The Weapons of Our Warfare (10:4) and Maclaren’s Strength in Weakness (12:8–9).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 2 Corinthians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

It is worth reading 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians together, as a story of one church and its apostle over several hard years, and then reading Romans, which Paul wrote from Corinth not long afterwards, when the reconciliation was complete and he was finally staying with them. The church that had caused him so much grief became the place from which he sent out his fullest account of the gospel.

But the best next step may be to take this letter into whatever is hardest in your own life, and to read it there. It was written by a man under pressure, at a loss and thrown down, and it was written for people like him:

So we do not give up. Our outer self may be decaying, but our inner self is being made new day after day. Our troubles are light and last only a moment, and they are bringing about for us an eternal glory, weighty beyond all measure. All the while, we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen. What can be seen lasts only a while; what cannot be seen is eternal.

— 2 Corinthians 4:16–18
